title: Judges 4:1–16
context: After Ehud’s death the cycle turns again: Israel does evil, and the LORD sells them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera has nine hundred chariots of iron and oppresses Israel for twenty years. Deborah, a prophetess who is already judging Israel, summons Barak and relays the LORD’s command to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor. Barak will go only if Deborah goes with him, and she agrees, while announcing that the honor of the victory will go to a woman. The battle at the Kishon ends with the LORD throwing Sisera’s army into confusion and Barak pursuing it to destruction. Both traditions see shared ground here: the LORD hands over and delivers, speaks through his prophet, and wins the battle himself, while human beings are called to trust and obey his word.

verses.text: The children of Israel again did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, when Ehud was dead.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel again does evil in the LORD’s sight after Ehud dies. The phrasing ties the renewed failure to the loss of the judge, as though the people’s faithfulness had leaned on his leadership.

Arminian readers see a people who did not internalize their loyalty to the LORD during the long rest. When the judge was gone, their own choices revealed where their hearts had drifted, and the cycle of unfaithfulness began again.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that eighty years of rest did not change Israel’s heart. Outward peace and a godly leader could restrain sin for a time, but they could not produce the lasting inner renewal that only God gives.

Both traditions agree that the verse marks the start of a new cycle and that Israel’s dependence on the judge exposes how shallow their covenant loyalty had become.

verses.text: The LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sells Israel into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigns in Hazor, with Sisera as his commander based in Harosheth of the Gentiles, whose location is uncertain. Hazor had been defeated under Joshua (Joshua 11), so its renewed power is notable.

Arminian readers see the loss of earlier gains as a consequence of unfaithfulness. What Israel had won in Joshua’s day is now turned against them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD sold Israel, so even a Canaanite king’s dominance is under God’s hand. The relation of this Jabin to the king in Joshua 11 is debated, and readers should hold the historical details with care.

Both traditions agree that the verse frames the oppression as God’s discipline, and that Sisera’s introduction prepares for the central conflict of the chapter.

verses.text: The children of Israel cried to the LORD, for he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and he mightily oppressed the children of Israel for twenty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel cries to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron and oppressed them severely for twenty years. The chariots represent overwhelming military power that Israel could not match.

Arminian readers note that the cry comes out of real distress after a long oppression. God allows his people to feel their helplessness so that they will turn to him, and he responds to that turning with deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the chariots of iron highlight Israel’s weakness and set the stage for a deliverance that will plainly be the LORD’s work. Human strength is clearly on Sisera’s side.

Both traditions agree that twenty years of oppression is the longest yet in the book, and that the cry is the hinge between Israel’s suffering and God’s answer through Deborah and Barak.

verses.text: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, judged Israel at that time.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deborah, a prophetess and the wife of Lappidoth, is judging Israel at this time. She is introduced as already serving, before any battle begins, as one who speaks for God and settles disputes.

Arminian readers note that God raises up a woman as prophet and judge in a patriarchal setting. Her role shows that God calls and uses those he chooses, and that faithful service is not limited to those the culture might expect.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that Deborah’s authority rests on God’s word; she is a prophetess first. Interpreters in both traditions differ on what her role implies for church leadership today, and that question should not be forced from the narrative alone.

Both traditions agree that Deborah is presented positively throughout, as a faithful servant through whom the LORD speaks and guides Israel at a critical moment.

verses.text: She lived under Deborah’s palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim; and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deborah sits under her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and Israel comes to her for judgment. Her role includes hearing cases and giving decisions.

Arminian readers see a picture of ordinary, faithful leadership. Before the battle, Deborah serves the people week by week, and the trust they place in her judgment prepares the way for her role in the deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the people come up to Deborah for judgment, suggesting that her decisions carry recognized authority grounded in God’s word. Her location in Ephraim places her at the center of Israel’s hill country.

Both traditions agree that the verse portrays a stable and respected ministry, and that Deborah’s faithful service in quiet times equips her to speak with authority when crisis comes.

verses.text: She sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedesh Naphtali, and said to him, “Hasn’t the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded, ‘Go and lead the way to Mount Tabor, and take with you ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?
verses.arminianNotes:
Deborah summons Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh Naphtali and reminds him that the LORD has commanded him to lead ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun to Mount Tabor. The command seems to have been given already.

Arminian readers note that Barak has received a word he has not yet acted on. Deborah calls him to obey what God has already told him, showing that God’s call invites a real and responsible human response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize that the command is the LORD’s, not Deborah’s; she speaks as his prophet. The battle plan, the place, and the forces are all set out by God before any human action is taken.

Both traditions agree that the verse shows God initiating the deliverance by his word, and that the WEB sentence continues into verse 7, where the promise of victory is completed.

verses.text: I will draw to you, to the river Kishon, Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into your hand.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD promises to draw Sisera, with his chariots and his multitude, to the river Kishon, and to deliver him into Barak’s hand. The verse completes the divine command begun in verse 6.

Arminian readers see a promise that calls for faith. God declares what he will do, and Barak is invited to trust that word enough to go into battle against an army that, by human measure, should overwhelm him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God will draw Sisera out; the enemy’s movements are under God’s direction. The LORD arranges the battlefield and guarantees the outcome before the armies meet.

Both traditions agree that the promise makes the deliverance the LORD’s work, and that the river Kishon will become the place where God overturns the advantage of Sisera’s chariots, as the Song in chapter 5 later celebrates.

verses.text: Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, then I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Barak tells Deborah he will go if she goes with him, but not otherwise. His condition reflects hesitation, though interpreters differ on how harshly to judge it.

Arminian readers see a real struggle of faith. Barak wants the assurance of God’s prophet beside him, which may be weakness, or a desire for God’s word to be present, and his choice shapes how the honor of the victory will fall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Barak’s hesitation shows that even those God uses are often weak in faith. Yet Barak is later listed among the faithful (Hebrews 11:32), so his faith, though imperfect, was real.

Both traditions agree that Barak’s condition should be read with nuance, neither excused nor caricatured, and that God works through his imperfect servants without approving every hesitation.

verses.text: She said, “I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the journey that you take won’t be for your honor; for the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman’s hand.” Deborah arose, and went with Barak to Kedesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deborah agrees to go but tells Barak that the honor will not be his, because the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman’s hand. She then goes with him to Kedesh.

Arminian readers see Barak’s choice carrying a real consequence. God still gives the victory, but the way Barak responded affects how the story unfolds, showing that human responses genuinely shape the course of events.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Deborah’s prophecy announces an outcome that God has already purposed. The reader may at first assume the woman is Deborah, but the story will reveal it to be Jael, displaying God’s sovereign direction.

Both traditions agree that the verse redirects honor away from human glory, and that the LORD remains the true source of the coming deliverance.

verses.text: Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali together to Kedesh. Ten thousand men followed him; and Deborah went up with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Barak calls Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh, ten thousand men follow him, and Deborah goes up with him. The army gathers exactly as the LORD commanded.

Arminian readers note that Barak, despite his hesitation, obeys. The men of Zebulun and Naphtali also respond to the summons, and their willing participation is part of how God brings about the promised victory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the army matches the number and tribes named in the LORD’s command in verse 6, so the plan God announced is now being carried out in detail.

Both traditions agree that the verse shows obedience to God’s word taking concrete form, and that Deborah’s presence fulfills her promise in verse 9. The Song in chapter 5 suggests that other tribes also responded, while some stayed away.

verses.text: Now Heber the Kenite had separated himself from the Kenites, even from the children of Hobab, Moses’ brother-in-law, and had pitched his tent as far as the oak in Zaanannim, which is by Kedesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator pauses to note that Heber the Kenite had separated from the other Kenites, descendants of Hobab, Moses’ brother-in-law, and had pitched his tent near the oak in Zaanannim by Kedesh. The aside prepares for Jael’s role.

Arminian readers note that Heber’s separation from his kin seems to have placed him near the conflict. Choices of alliance and location matter in this story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the aside as a quiet signal that God’s providence is arranging the circumstances for the outcome Deborah foretold. The Kenites had longstanding ties to Israel through Moses’ family.

Both traditions agree that this verse, which might seem a digression, is essential to understanding the end of the chapter. The exact location of Zaanannim is uncertain, and readers should not press the geography too far.

verses.text: They told Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sisera is told that Barak son of Abinoam has gone up to Mount Tabor. The report sets the enemy in motion exactly as the LORD had said he would draw Sisera out.

Arminian readers note that Sisera acts on information he receives, making his own decisions as commander. Yet those decisions lead him toward the place where God has promised to defeat him, showing God working through real human choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in this report the fulfillment of God’s word that he would draw Sisera to the Kishon. Even the enemy’s intelligence reports serve God’s purpose.

Both traditions agree that the verse shows how God’s promise in verse 7 begins to come true through ordinary events.

verses.text: Sisera gathered together all his chariots, even nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people who were with him, from Harosheth of the Gentiles, to the river Kishon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sisera gathers all nine hundred iron chariots and all his people from Harosheth of the Gentiles to the river Kishon. The full strength of the oppressor is brought to the field.

Arminian readers note that Sisera brings his best military assets, confident in his strength. The scene invites Barak and Israel to trust God’s word even when facing a force that seems overwhelming by every human measure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers observe that the gathering of the chariots at the Kishon is exactly what God promised to bring about. The enemy’s greatest strength is assembled in the very place where God will overthrow it.

Both traditions agree that the repetition of the nine hundred chariots of iron emphasizes the odds against Israel, and so emphasizes that the coming victory will be the LORD’s doing.

verses.text: Deborah said to Barak, “Go; for this is the day in which the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Hasn’t the LORD gone out before you?” So Barak went down from Mount Tabor, and ten thousand men after him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Deborah tells Barak to go, because this is the day the LORD has delivered Sisera into his hand, and asks whether the LORD has not gone out before him. Barak goes down from Tabor with ten thousand men.

Arminian readers see faith acting on God’s word at the decisive moment. Barak moves when the prophet speaks, and his descent from the mountain is a real act of trust in God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress Deborah’s words that the LORD has delivered Sisera and has gone out before Barak. The battle is already won in God’s purpose before Israel engages, and the LORD leads his army as its true commander.

Both traditions agree that the verse is the turning point of the chapter, uniting God’s promise and Israel’s obedience as Barak leads the men down to the plain.

verses.text: The LORD confused Sisera, all his chariots, and all his army, with the edge of the sword before Barak. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled away on his feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD confuses Sisera, his chariots, and his army before Barak, and Sisera abandons his chariot and flees on foot. The great military advantage collapses.

Arminian readers note that God intervenes directly, yet Barak and his men still fight with the sword. Divine action and human effort work together, and the commander who trusted his chariots now runs on foot.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers emphasize that it is the LORD who confused Sisera’s army. The Song in chapter 5 suggests that the forces of nature, including the Kishon itself, were involved (Judges 5:20–21), though the details are poetic and should be read with care.

Both traditions agree that the LORD is the decisive actor in the victory, and that the chariots in which Sisera trusted became useless before God.

verses.text: But Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth of the Gentiles; and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword. There was not a man left.
verses.arminianNotes:
Barak pursues the chariots and the army to Harosheth of the Gentiles, and Sisera’s whole army falls by the sword, with no one left. The rout is complete.

Arminian readers note that Barak follows through on the victory God has given, pursuing the enemy to its base. Faithful obedience carries the task to completion rather than stopping at the first sign of success.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the total defeat as the fulfillment of God’s promise to deliver Sisera’s army into Barak’s hand. The thoroughness of the defeat shows that the LORD’s word does not fail.

Both traditions agree that the verse concludes the battle narrative, while leaving Sisera himself still at large, so that the story turns to his fate and to the woman into whose hand God would sell him.
